title: Geometric Ginzburg-Landau theory of charge ordering and commensurability
authors: Aneesh Agarwal, Rutvij Gholap, Mohammad Saeed Bahramy, Robert-Jan Slager
abstract: The concept of quantum geometry has recently led to reinvigorated insights in a wide range of fields including physical responses, superconductivity, and optical transitions, with effects most pronounced in systems with nearly flat dispersion. Here, we show that it plays an essential role in charge density wave formation (CDW) -- an important physical phenomenon that is responsible for driving various sharp changes in material transport properties including metal-insulator transitions. We derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau theory including uncharted contributions and, as a highlight, discover a general criterion for both CDW formation and commensurability transitions where underlying electron-phonon interactions manifest purely as electronic quantum geometric enhancements/suppressions. We benchmark our framework in a class of transition-metal dichalcogenides and resolve a longstanding puzzle where well-established purely kinetic CDW criteria fail in describing the correct ordering wavevector. Besides rendering robust criteria and fundamental insights that are immediately relevant to several experimental charge ordering systems, our theory can also be applied directly to other phonon-mediated phases such as superconductivity, and can be used as an important tool to explore the interplay between various such states. More generally, our framework provides a recipe for investigating the role of quantum geometry in phase transitions.
summary: This paper develops a geometric Ginzburg-Landau theory to explain Charge Density Wave (CDW) formation in materials like TMDs. It shows that quantum geometry provides essential, previously uncaptured contributions to the phase transition free energy. The resulting theory yields robust criteria that successfully predict CDW ordering wavevectors where conventional electronic models fail.
main_problem: Deriving a geometric Ginzburg-Landau theory to accurately describe Charge Density Wave (CDW) formation and commensurability transitions, especially in systems where standard electronic criteria fail.
main_result: The theory establishes that quantum geometry plays an essential role, providing a general criterion for CDW formation that successfully predicts ordering wavevectors in TMDs where simpler models fail.
method: The authors derive an effective Ginzburg-Landau functional by integrating out phonon degrees of freedom from an electron-phonon Hamiltonian, leading to modified susceptibility tensors.
model_or_system: The work focuses on Charge Density Waves (CDWs) in Transition Metal Dichalcogenides (TMDs) with hexagonal lattices, utilizing a Ginzburg-Landau framework expanded to include higher-order geometric terms.
key_observables: The CDW driver ($\Theta_Q$), the quadratic susceptibility tensor ($\chi$), and the coefficients of the GL functional ($\Pi_Q, |\gamma_Q|,  eta_Q$).
important_parameters: The wavevector $Q$, the lattice symmetry ($C_3$), and the relative strength of quantum geometric enhancements versus bare susceptibility.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the coupling function $g_q$ is flat over relevant $q$ states to isolate electronic contributions, and that the system can be reduced to a scalar order parameter due to susceptibility anisotropy.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the geometric mechanism for CDW formation using three symmetry-related wavevectors in hexagonal systems, and plot the CDW driver ($\Theta_Q$) for various TMDs, showing geometric enhancements selecting the correct wavevector.
paper_structure: The paper builds from deriving the geometric GL theory for CDW instability, establishing the general criterion, benchmarking it on TMDs, and refining the theory by including higher-order terms (like sextic terms) to resolve discrepancies in the predicted ordering wavevector.
why_interesting: The explicit incorporation of quantum geometry into a phase transition theory provides a powerful, generalizable tool for understanding how subtle electronic structure effects dictate macroscopic material properties like CDW formation, which is relevant to many strongly correlated systems.
